# Discussion

Bat activity varied substantially across the sampling period, among sites, and in relation to nightly environmental conditions. By combining site-specific seasonal phenology with environmental models informed by an explicit causal framework, we were able to distinguish broad seasonal variation from associations with temperature, relative humidity, and lunar phase. Three findings were particularly important. First, seasonal activity differed markedly among sites, indicating substantial local variation in the timing and magnitude of seasonal bat activity. Second, activity increased with temperature across all three echolocation-frequency groups, although the magnitude of this response differed among groups. Third, and most consistent with our mechanistic prediction, sensitivity to relative humidity increased across frequency groups: humidity had little detectable negative association with low-frequency activity, a moderate negative association with mid-frequency activity, and a pronounced negative association with high-frequency activity. Together, these results indicate that environmental variation can structure bat activity through processes operating at multiple temporal and biological scales, including a pattern consistent with frequency-dependent atmospheric attenuation.

## Seasonal phenology and nightly environmental conditions

Seasonal variation in bat activity reflected both changes in nightly environmental conditions and seasonal processes not captured by those conditions. The substantial difference between the overall and environmentally conditioned seasonal patterns indicates that apparent phenology in acoustic activity can partly emerge from the strong seasonal covariance between weather and bat activity. This is consistent with studies showing that temperature and other weather conditions structure nightly bat activity across temperate systems [@bender2015; @jorge2021; @mas2022; @russoPetrick2023; @wolbert2014]. At the same time, a pronounced seasonal signal remained after accounting for temperature, relative humidity, and lunar phase, indicating that weather alone does not account for seasonal changes in activity. Migration and other seasonal changes in behavior can generate pronounced shifts in the distribution and activity of temperate bats [@cryan2003; @weller2016], while reproductive phenology, changes in prey communities, and seasonal shifts in roosting and habitat use may contribute additional temporal structure. Seasonal activity should therefore be viewed not simply as a response to changing weather, but as the combined outcome of environmental conditions and biological phenology.

The strong among-site differences in seasonal phenology further demonstrate that these processes operate at local as well as regional scales. Sites exposed to the same broad climatic season nevertheless differed substantially in the timing and magnitude of activity. Local habitat conditions, proximity to roosts, resource availability, species composition, and seasonal changes in landscape use could all generate such differences. Consequently, a regional seasonal trajectory may obscure biologically meaningful spatial variation in phenology, even when monitoring sites are geographically close. This spatial heterogeneity may be particularly important in acoustic monitoring studies, where seasonal changes in the species using individual sites can produce very different local activity trajectories within the same regional bat assemblage.

Accounting for this local phenology is also important when estimating associations with nightly environmental conditions. Temperature and humidity vary seasonally at the same time that bat populations undergo changes in migration, reproduction, energetic requirements, and habitat use. Environmental associations can therefore incorporate multiple processes if seasonal structure is inadequately represented. Our results suggest that explicitly representing local seasonal trajectories can help distinguish this phenological variation from associations with nightly environmental conditions.

## Humidity and echolocation frequency

The clearest evidence for frequency-dependent environmental sensitivity emerged for relative humidity. Across approximately the 10th to 90th percentiles of observed relative humidity (49–85%), expected activity changed little in the low-frequency group, from 4.3 to 5.3 five-minute detection intervals per night. In contrast, expected activity declined from 19.8 to 13.7 intervals in the mid-frequency group and from 52.4 to 29.0 intervals in the high-frequency group. These changes corresponded to an estimated activity ratio of 1.23 for the low-frequency group, 0.69 for the mid-frequency group, and 0.55 for the high-frequency group. The low-frequency contrast was uncertain, whereas posterior support for declining activity was strong in both the mid- and high-frequency groups.

This ordering is consistent with the prediction that atmospheric conditions should disproportionately influence the transmission of higher-frequency ultrasound. Atmospheric absorption increases with ultrasonic frequency and varies with humidity, causing higher-frequency calls to lose energy more rapidly during propagation [@griffin1971; @lawrence1982]. Increased attenuation can reduce the distance over which an echolocating bat detects prey or other environmental features and may therefore alter the profitability of foraging under particular atmospheric conditions. Experimental and modeling studies further indicate that atmospheric conditions can affect prey-detection distance and that bats may not completely compensate for increased attenuation through adjustments in call structure [@deframond2023; @luo2014].

The field pattern observed here extends that mechanistic prediction from acoustic propagation to assemblage-level activity. The magnitude of the humidity association increased in the same order as characteristic echolocation frequency, with the strongest decline occurring among species using the highest-frequency calls. Importantly, the low-frequency group did not simply show a weaker version of the high-frequency response; its estimated activity was approximately stable across the central humidity gradient. This contrast is consistent with the expectation that relatively low-frequency calls experience less humidity-sensitive attenuation than higher-frequency calls.

Our observational design cannot establish atmospheric attenuation as the sole cause of these differences. Humidity may also influence insect availability, thermoregulation, vegetation moisture, or other aspects of foraging conditions, and frequency groups contain species differing in ecological characteristics beyond echolocation frequency. Nevertheless, several features make the attenuation hypothesis particularly relevant. The frequency ordering was specified from acoustic principles rather than derived from the observed activity patterns, the response was evaluated after accounting for temperature and seasonal phenology, and the magnitude of the negative association increased across the frequency gradient in the predicted direction. The resulting correspondence between an a priori physical mechanism and field activity therefore provides evidence that atmospheric transmission may contribute to community-level responses to humidity without requiring the stronger conclusion that attenuation alone produced the observed pattern.

## Temperature and thermal responses

Temperature was strongly positively associated with activity across all three frequency groups. Across the central 80% of observed nightly temperatures, approximately 6–17°C, expected activity increased from 1.5 to 13.7 five-minute intervals per night in the low-frequency group, from 3.5 to 69.9 intervals in the mid-frequency group, and from 33.9 to 68.3 intervals in the high-frequency group. Posterior support for increasing activity across this temperature range was strong for all three groups, although the magnitude and shape of the responses differed.

Positive associations between temperature and bat activity are widely reported in temperate systems [@bender2015; @jorge2021; @mas2022; @russoPetrick2023; @wolbert2014]. Temperature can influence nightly activity through several pathways. Warmer conditions may increase aerial insect abundance and activity, reduce thermoregulatory costs, and increase the energetic profitability of emergence and foraging. Conversely, cool nights can reduce prey availability while increasing the energetic costs of maintaining body temperature. The strong positive responses observed here are therefore consistent with multiple, potentially interacting physiological and trophic mechanisms.

The differences among frequency groups should not, however, be interpreted as direct effects of echolocation frequency on thermal sensitivity. Unlike the physical connection between call frequency and atmospheric attenuation, there is no equivalent direct mechanism linking characteristic call frequency to temperature response. Frequency groups aggregate species that also differ in body size, wing morphology, migratory behavior, roosting ecology, habitat use, and foraging strategy. Their temperature curves therefore describe assemblage-level responses of groups defined by acoustic characteristics rather than physiological thermal guilds.

This distinction also changes the biological interpretation relative to simpler formulations of the analysis. Earlier model structures suggested an unusual cool-temperature response among high-frequency bats, which could have invited an interpretation based on cold tolerance in small-bodied *Myotis* [@audet1996; @lausen2003; @tuttle1974]. That pattern did not persist after correcting the sampling frame and representing site-specific seasonal phenology. Instead, the final models indicated increasing activity with temperature in all three frequency groups. This illustrates the importance of adequately representing sampling effort and seasonal structure before assigning ecological mechanisms to apparent environmental response curves.

## Lunar phase

Lunar phase was a weaker and less consistent correlate of activity than temperature or relative humidity. The strongest evidence occurred in the high-frequency group, where expected activity increased from approximately 37.8 five-minute intervals per night near the new moon to 48.3 intervals near the full moon, corresponding to an activity ratio of 1.28. In contrast, the estimated new- to full-moon difference was small and uncertain in the low-frequency group, and evidence for an increase in the mid-frequency group was also comparatively weak.

The literature on lunar effects in bats is notably variable, with studies reporting reduced activity under brighter lunar conditions, increased activity, or little detectable response [@morrison1978; @hecker1999; @karlsson2002; @milne2005; @saldanavazquez2013]. Proposed mechanisms include changes in predation risk, prey behavior, illumination, habitat structure, and foraging strategy. Our results provide little support for a single community-wide response to lunar phase. Instead, the positive association in the high-frequency group and weak responses in the other groups suggest that any lunar effect was contingent on assemblage composition or ecological characteristics correlated with frequency group.

As with the other environmental predictors, the lunar estimates are conditional associations rather than experimental effects. Their interpretation is strengthened, however, by accounting for seasonal phenology and nightly weather simultaneously. Because lunar phase progresses independently of the seasonal weather cycle but can still become associated with environmental conditions within a finite sampling period, incorporating these sources of variation provides a clearer estimate of lunar-associated changes in activity than an unadjusted comparison among moon phases.

## Model adequacy and temporal structure

The analytical development also highlights two methodological considerations relevant to long-duration passive acoustic monitoring. First, nights on which a detector did not operate cannot be treated as ecological zeroes. Reconstructing detector effort showed that some apparent zero-activity site-nights reflected missing acoustic sampling rather than sampled nights without bat detections. We therefore excluded nights lacking evidence that the detector operated while retaining legitimate zeroes on sampled nights. This distinction is fundamental when environmental conditions are available continuously but biological observations depend on equipment that can fail intermittently. Otherwise, equipment failure can become embedded in seasonal trajectories and environmental response functions as apparent biological absence.

Second, overdispersion and temporal dependence represented distinct aspects of model inadequacy. A negative-binomial observation model accommodated the substantial variation in nightly activity but did not by itself eliminate persistent temporal autocorrelation. The major improvement occurred when seasonal phenology was allowed to vary among sites. In the final aggregate environmental model, residual autocorrelation declined from 0.379 at a one-day lag to 0.208 at two days and 0.168 at three days, approached zero by four days, and remained weak at longer lags. Thus, remaining dependence was concentrated primarily at the shortest temporal scales.

We did not add an autoregressive process solely to eliminate this residual short-lag correlation. The final model represented the major ecological and sampling processes relevant to our questions, substantially reduced the longer-range temporal dependence, and reproduced the principal features of the observed activity distribution in posterior predictive checks. Some discrepancies in predictive variance remained among sites, but the model recovered site-specific mean activity well and provided adequate representation of the response features relevant to the environmental contrasts. In this setting, additional complexity intended primarily to reproduce every feature of the observed data would not necessarily improve inference about the ecological quantities of interest.

More generally, the reduction in temporal dependence after incorporating site-specific phenology illustrates a useful distinction for ecological time series. Autocorrelation in residuals does not necessarily imply that an autoregressive process is the missing biological mechanism. When repeated sites follow different seasonal trajectories, observations close together in time can remain systematically similar because important ecological heterogeneity has not been represented. Flexible representation of that heterogeneity may therefore be more informative than imposing a common temporal correlation process.

## Ecological implications

The contrasting responses among frequency groups suggest that environmental conditions can reorganize nightly bat activity through several mechanisms operating simultaneously. Temperature was positively associated with activity throughout the assemblage, consistent with broad effects on bat energetics and prey availability. Humidity, in contrast, produced a distinctly frequency-ordered response consistent with differences in ultrasonic transmission. Lunar phase produced weaker and less uniform responses. These patterns indicate that environmental change need not affect all components of a bat assemblage in parallel, even when species occupy the same landscape and experience the same nightly weather.

The humidity result may be particularly relevant when considering changes in climatic conditions. If high-frequency foragers experience greater acoustic constraints under humid conditions, changes in the frequency or duration of humid nights could alter when environmental conditions are favorable for different components of the assemblage. Such effects would occur alongside temperature-mediated changes in prey activity, energetic costs, and seasonal phenology. Predicting responses to environmental change therefore requires considering not only whether overall bat activity increases or decreases, but also whether environmental conditions alter the relative activity of species with different sensory and ecological characteristics.

Our results also emphasize that passive acoustic activity is the product of both animal behavior and the observation process. Atmospheric conditions can potentially influence whether and how bats forage while simultaneously influencing how sound propagates between a calling bat and a detector. Consequently, acoustic activity should not automatically be interpreted as abundance, and environmentally structured variation in detections may arise through several pathways. Grouping species according to a mechanistically relevant acoustic characteristic provides one way to evaluate these processes, particularly when predictions about the direction and relative magnitude of environmental responses can be specified in advance.

More broadly, this study demonstrates the value of making both the estimand and the assumed causal structure explicit when analyzing correlated environmental predictors. Day of year, temperature, and humidity do not vary independently, and including them together in a statistical model does not by itself determine the ecological quantity represented by each coefficient or smooth. Combining causal reasoning with flexible nonlinear models, explicit sampling effort, and local seasonal phenology allowed us to distinguish overall seasonal variation from conditional environmental associations and to evaluate mechanistically motivated predictions at the assemblage level.

Together, our results show that nightly bat activity reflects environmental processes operating through multiple mechanisms and at different temporal scales. Local seasonal phenology accounted for substantial temporal structure that was obscured when sites were assumed to share a common seasonal trajectory, while temperature was strongly and positively associated with activity across echolocation-frequency groups. Most notably, sensitivity to relative humidity increased across frequency groups in the direction predicted from frequency-dependent atmospheric attenuation. Although observational data cannot isolate acoustic attenuation from every correlated ecological or detection process, the correspondence between an a priori physical prediction and the frequency-ordered field response provides evidence that atmospheric transmission may contribute to community-level patterns of bat activity. Explicitly separating seasonal phenology, nightly environmental conditions, sampling effort, and mechanistically motivated assemblage structure therefore provides a more interpretable framework for understanding environmental variation in passive acoustic monitoring data.
